notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes for 1 Samuel 20:1–21, compiled from the available sources.

---

## Notes on 1 Samuel 20:1–21

### v. 1 — David Flees to Jonathan

- **David fled from Naioth in Ramah:** While Saul lay under the prophetic ecstasy described in chapter 19, David escaped. He returned secretly to Gibeah (Saul's royal residence) to consult Jonathan. The Pulpit Commentary suggests that Saul's experience at Naioth may have produced a temporary softening, leading David to hope reconciliation was possible — hence David expected to dine at the king's table at the New Moon (v. 5). Yet David remained deeply wary.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/

- **"What have I done? What is my iniquity?…":** David's threefold question protests his innocence. Gill notes that David speaks as one who must be guilty of some very great crime — yet is conscious of none. Ellicott adds that David's words here echo the language of several Psalms, where he maintains how bitterly he has been wronged despite his righteousness.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **David was testing Jonathan's loyalty:** Enduring Word notes that David wanted to know whether Jonathan had come to agree with his father Saul. More than Saul's heart, David needed to know Jonathan's heart.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/

- **Spurgeon** observed: "David had an enemy upon the throne; and God gave him a friend in the heir to the throne. If thou hast an enemy, thou hast also a friend; God sets the one over against the other."
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-20-commentary

---

### v. 2 — Jonathan's Disbelief

- **"Far from it! You shall not die":** Jonathan could not believe his father truly intended to kill David. Gill notes that Jonathan attributed Saul's violent outbursts to his "frenzy" and "melancholy disorder," thinking David had nothing to fear when Saul was in his right mind. Ellicott likewise says Jonathan put all that had happened down to his father's "unhappy malady."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"My father does nothing…without telling me":** The Hebrew phrase is literally "without uncovering my ear" — a private disclosure (Pulpit Commentary). Jonathan argues that Saul always confided state secrets to him. The Pulpit notes that Saul's rash talk about killing David in 19:1 actually confirms Jonathan's claim about his father's openness.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-20.html

- **Jonathan's loyalty to his father is praised:** Spurgeon commented, "One admires Jonathan for defending Saul; he will not believe anything bad of his father. Children should never believe anything evil of their parents unless it is forced upon them; this rule is a part of the command, 'Honour thy father and thy mother.'"
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-20-commentary

---

### v. 3 — David's Oath: "There Is But a Step Between Me and Death"

- **David's insight into Saul:** David explains that Saul deliberately hid his plans from Jonathan because Saul knew of the friendship between the two and did not wish to grieve his son. Ellicott remarks that David, "with his clear, bright intellect, looked deeper into Saul's heart than did the heroic, guileless son."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"There is but a step between me and death":** David felt his death was inevitable. Enduring Word describes it as walking "on a slippery plank over a great canyon." Gill enumerates the narrow escapes: Saul's javelin (18:11), messengers sent to David's house (19:11), messengers to Naioth (19:20), and Saul coming himself (19:22). Spurgeon added, "Yesterday I was born: today I live: tomorrow I must die."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-20-commentary

---

### v. 4 — Jonathan's Blank-Cheque Promise

- **"Whatever you desire, I will do for you":** Now convinced of the danger, Jonathan offers David his full help. Enduring Word notes that Jonathan could have rebuked David for lack of faith ("Where is your faith, brother?"), but instead offered practical assistance to a discouraged friend. Gill says Jonathan was willing to speak to his father, hide David, or pursue any method David chose.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 5 — The New Moon Feast and David's Plan

- **"Tomorrow is the New Moon":** The first day of the month was a festival with special sacrifices (Numbers 28:11–15; 10:10) and a state banquet at Saul's court at which David, as the king's son-in-law and a high-ranking officer, was expected to attend. Gill notes some Jewish traditions suggest this particular New Moon may also have been the Feast of Trumpets (New Year's Day).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"Let me go and hide in the field until the third evening":** David proposes to absent himself from court for three days while Jonathan observes Saul's reaction. Gill explains the third evening would be the evening of the second day of the month, counting from the evening of their conversation.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 6 — The Excuse: A Family Sacrifice at Bethlehem

- **"David urgently requested my permission to hurry to Bethlehem…":** David instructs Jonathan to tell Saul that David went to an annual clan sacrifice. Gill argues this may have been true — David could have gone to Bethlehem after hiding, returning in time to meet Jonathan on the third day. Ellicott, however, is more cautious: the Mosaic Law required such feasts at the central sanctuary (Deuteronomy 12:5), but since Shiloh had been destroyed, family usages "contrary to the (Mosaic) prescriptions" had established themselves. Ellicott adds: "It is, however, clear that David did not purpose being present at it, and therefore the excuse was a feigned one. The morality of this request of David is by no means sanctioned by the compiler of the history; he simply relates the story."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 7 — The Test: Saul's Reaction

- **"If he says, 'Good,' then your servant is safe…":** David proposes a simple diagnostic: Saul's calm acceptance means reconciliation; fury means determined evil. Gill explains that if Saul were merely disappointed, it would show goodwill; but "if he be very wroth" it would prove "a settled obstinate malice in his heart."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 8 — "Deal Faithfully…If There Is Iniquity in Me, Kill Me Yourself"

- **"You have brought me into a covenant of the LORD with you":** David appeals to the solemn covenant Jonathan had initiated (1 Samuel 18:3). The Pulpit Commentary says that because this covenant was "cemented by the invocation of the name of Jehovah," David could expect not just one act of kindness but constant faithfulness.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"If there is iniquity in me, kill me yourself":** David is so confident of his innocence that he would rather die at Jonathan's hand than be handed over to Saul. Enduring Word notes David was shaken that Jonathan had not warned him about Saul's pursuit to Naioth, and here he essentially says: "If you really are working for your father and agree I deserve to die, then just kill me now." Ellicott adds that this "supposes that Jonathan had the right to inflict capital punishment for crimes against his father as king."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 9 — Jonathan's Protestation of Loyalty

- **"Never!…If I ever found out…would I not tell you?":** Jonathan indignantly rejects the suggestion that he would conceal evil from David. Ellicott notes the Hebrew here is broken and incomplete — "They betoken the agitation and deep feeling of the chivalrous, indignant speaker."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

---

### vv. 10–11 — "Who Will Tell Me?" / They Go to the Field

- **"Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?"** David raises a practical difficulty: if Saul's response is hostile, how will Jonathan get the dangerous message to David? Ellicott notes the Hebrew here is "very abrupt and involved. Evidently the very words uttered in the memorable scene by the excited and sorrowful friends are remembered and reported."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"Come, let us go out into the field":** They leave the palace for privacy to discuss the matter freely, out of earshot of Saul's servants.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/

---

### vv. 12–13 — Jonathan's Solemn Oath

- **"By the LORD, the God of Israel, I will sound out my father…":** The phrase is an oath formula. The Pulpit Commentary notes that some Hebrew manuscripts supply "As Jehovah the God of Israel liveth." Ellicott says the vocative "O Lord God of Israel" is unusual, and versions handle it variously: the Syriac reads "The Lord of Israel is my witness," the LXX reads "The Lord God of Israel knows." Jonathan commits to discover Saul's heart and report back.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"By this time tomorrow or the next day":** The Pulpit Commentary clarifies the timing: "By this time on the third morrow." The conversation happens before the New Moon; the next day is the feast; the day after that is the "third day" (the morrow after the second feast day).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"May the LORD punish me…if I do not tell you":** Jonathan places himself under a curse if he fails to warn David. If the news is good, he will send a messenger; if evil, he will come himself.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/

- **"May the LORD be with you, as He has been with my father":** Enduring Word notes Jonathan's spiritual maturity here — he recognizes that God was "for" Saul in the sense of offering him opportunities for repentance, even though Saul was rejecting them.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/

---

### vv. 14–15 — Jonathan's Request: Loving Devotion for His House

- **"Treat me with the LORD's loving devotion, that I may not die":** The Hebrew of verses 14–15 is notoriously difficult. Ellicott reports that several scholars (Maurer, Ewald, Keil, Lange) emend the text by changing *v'lo* ("and not") to *v'lu* ("and O that" / "would that"), yielding: "And mayest thou, if I still live, show to me the favour of the Lord, and if I die, not withdraw thy favour from my house for ever." Jonathan was looking ahead to his own premature death.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"Do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household":** Jonathan knew that when a new dynasty replaced an old one, it was customary in the ancient Near East for the new king to kill all potential claimants from the former royal house. Jonathan foresaw David's eventual kingship and wanted protection for his descendants. This reflects Jonathan's full recognition of David's destiny.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 16 — Covenant with the House of David

- **"So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David":** Ellicott notes this is best read not as part of the dialogue but as a remark interposed by the narrator. The literal Hebrew is: "So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, and Jehovah required it at the hand of David's enemies." Gill explains that Jonathan invoked the LORD as avenger on whichever side broke the covenant — whether Jonathan's descendants or David's.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 17 — Sworn Again Out of Love

- **"Jonathan had David reaffirm his vow out of love for him":** Gill explains that Jonathan — having sworn himself — "moved and insisted on it, that David should swear to keep covenant with him, and his family." Ellicott adds: "Throughout this touching interview it is the prince who appears as the suppliant for the outlaw's future kind offices. Jonathan — looking forward with absolute certainty to the day when his persecuted friend would be on the throne, and he in his grave — dreaded for his own fatherless children the fate which too probably awaited them."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"For Jonathan loved David as he loved himself":** This echoes 1 Samuel 18:1. Gaebelein notes: "Both were men of faith putting their trust in Jehovah and hence this great affection."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 18 — The Empty Seat

- **"Tomorrow is the New Moon, and you will be missed if your seat is empty":** Jonathan confirms the plan. David's place at the banquet table would be conspicuously vacant. Gill explains David would be "inquired after, because not in his usual place at mealtime."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 19 — The Stone Ezel

- **"When you have stayed three days, hurry down to the place you hid…":** The Hebrew here is challenging. Ellicott notes that the word translated "quickly" (Hebrew *m'od*) more literally means "greatly," and Dean Payne Smith renders it: "on the third day go a long way down into the valley" — meaning David should be far from prying eyes, not necessarily moving fast.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"On the day this trouble began":** The Hebrew phrase *b'yom hammaăseh* ("on the day of the deed") is obscure. Gesenius, De Wette, and Maurer take "the deed" to refer to Saul's design to kill David (cf. 19:2).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

- **"The stone Ezel":** This stone (or cairn, or possibly ruin) is mentioned nowhere else in Scripture. Some suppose it was a road-stone or guide-post. The LXX reads *argab* or *ergab*, meaning "a heap of stones." Ewald, slightly emending the text, understands it as "the lonely waste." Gill notes that the name Ezel means "going," leading Jewish commentators to see it as a directional marker for travellers, though this might make it too public a place for David's hiding — hence others think it was named for David and Jonathan's habit of "going" there to talk.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html

---

### v. 20 — Three Arrows

- **"I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as if I were aiming at a target":** Jonathan would come out after the feast, apparently for archery practice, with a servant boy. The arrows would be shot near the stone Ezel where David hid. Gill suggests three arrows corresponded to the three days David was absent.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/

---

### v. 21 — The Signal: "The Arrows Are on This Side of You"

- **The coded message:** Jonathan would call out to his servant boy. If he said, "Look, the arrows are on this side of you; bring them" (i.e., between Jonathan and the mark), David would know it was safe to return. This pre-arranged signal allowed communication even if Jonathan were accompanied by Saul's men from the city. As it happened, Jonathan came alone with just his servant, but the sign was used anyway to draw David's attention before their final farewell (vv. 35–42).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/

- **"As surely as the LORD lives, it is safe for you and there is no danger":** Jonathan's assurance is given under oath. Gill comments: "he might appear, and not be afraid of being seen by any, since by this sign he might be assured that Saul was well affected to him."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html

---

## Tradition-Specific Observations

**Reformed / Covenantal (Ligonier / Gospel Coalition):** Ligonier's devotional stresses the covenant aspect of the chapter — that oaths and vows "exist to help prevent us from sinning against one another," and that Jonathan's loyalty meant "he would have to forgo loyalty to his own family for the sake of doing what was right." The Gospel Coalition notes that Jonathan "stays in town with his father" because "we choose our friends, but we do not choose our family; yet our responsibilities to our families take a prior claim."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/davids-great-friendship
— https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/1-samuel-20-1-corinthians-2-lamentations-5-psalm-36/

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises the practical-application dimension: Jonathan modelled genuine support to a discouraged friend; David's "bleak road" was God's appointed path to teach him total dependence. Guzik also ties the arrow signal to the theme that "sometimes a small thing pivots a person's entire life."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/

**Baptist (Spurgeon / Gill):** Spurgeon uniquely applies this text to encourage Christians who face hostile authorities: "David had an enemy upon the throne; and God gave him a friend in the heir to the throne… God sets the one over against the other in his providence." Spurgeon also used v. 3 evangelistically, asking hearers to consider how close they are to death and eternity. Gill provides detailed philological and rabbinic notes (e.g., on the New Moon possibly being the Feast of Trumpets, and Jewish interpretations of "Ezel").
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-20-commentary
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott is notably cautious about the morality of David's excuse in v. 6: "It is, however, clear that David did not purpose being present at it, and therefore the excuse was a feigned one. The morality of this request of David is by no means sanctioned by the compiler of the history; he simply relates the story." He also provides the most detailed textual notes on the difficult Hebrew of vv. 14–15 and 19.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html

**Pulpit Commentary:** Suggests Samuel mediated a temporary reconciliation after Naioth, which explains why David's place was expected at the feast. On v. 8, emphasises the covenant as cemented by Jehovah's name, making it "firm and assured."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-20.html
